You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===

Interviewee: I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order. I add new drones to our fleet, retire old ones, set up charging pads at our sites, and take drones out of service for repairs before putting them back. I also send drones to charge, and regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Walk me through a normal working day for you, from the moment you start to the moment you finish.

Interviewee: I plan and run flights as a dispatcher, taking legal responsibility for deciding which drone flies and along which way before signing off a flight. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can call off a flight. Before and during a flight, things happen outside my control like whether the load is ready or how the drone reaches its points, while closure zones and sudden closures announced by authorities might come into force while my drones are already in the air.

Interviewer: You said you sign off flights and can call them off. Take me through one ordinary morning: what do you look at first, and what happens between that and the moment a specific flight is signed off?

Interviewee: I look at help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, since software never chooses a drone or a way for us. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I decide which drone flies and along which way. Finally, I sign off a flight before it leaves, though I can also call it off.

Interviewer: Think of one specific flight you signed off recently. What was the first thing you looked at for that job, and where did you look it up?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's make it easier: think about the last time you were about to send a drone to a site and you had to choose between drones or routes. What did you do first, before you chose anything?

Interviewee: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. Software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones.

Interviewer: When you say a drone "could get to" a job start, what exactly do you check to decide that?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's move to a different question. Think about the worst day you've had in the last few months. What happened, from the start of the day to the moment it got bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've noticed that a few of my questions have gotten "I don't know," and your answers keep returning to the same few points. Is there something about these questions that's hard to answer, or would a different way of asking help more?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try something more concrete. Who do you most often pass work to after you've signed off a flight, and what do you send them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's come at it from another side. If someone built a new system to help you plan flights, what is the one thing you'd be most worried it would get wrong?

Interviewee: I worry about the service being restarted or updated during working hours while drones are flying, or crashing, though we accept a few minutes of interruption. I also worry that the links used to give instructions to drones and charging equipment are unreliable, meaning an instruction might get through twice and the sender often cannot tell if the first attempt arrived. Furthermore, radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, which means reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

Interviewer: You mentioned an instruction might get through twice, and the sender often can't tell whether the first attempt arrived. Tell me about the last time that happened. What did you see, and what did you do?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's take a hypothetical instead. Suppose a drone you've signed off loses its link partway through a flight. What is the first thing you would want to know in the next minute?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything you check by hand, even though the system already shows you an answer?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Do you pass work to the fleet technicians or the airspace desk, or they pass work to you? Tell me which one happens more often.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I'm not getting enough detail yet to cover the main parts of your work. Would you prefer to answer some of these questions in writing, or to come back at another time when it's easier to talk through them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try a different kind of question. What part of your work do you find easiest to explain to someone new?

Interviewee: I plan and run flights, and I am the licensed person responsible for each flight who decides which drone flies along which way before signing off a flight. I also have the power to call off a flight.

Interviewer: What usually leads you to call off a flight? Describe the last time you did it, or a time you came close.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: If you could change one thing about how flights get planned and called off today, what would it be?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Would it help if I only asked yes-or-no questions from here on?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Do you keep a written checklist or log when you sign off a flight? Yes or no is fine.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there a colleague who knows the planning work well and might be easier to talk with about it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewee: I don't know.

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day on the airspace desk, from the moment you start to the moment you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's make it smaller. What is the first thing you look at when you sit down this morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's start from something more concrete. Think of the last time you received an airspace notice or change. What was it about, and how did it reach you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've asked three questions and each time you've said you don't know, so I may be asking the wrong thing. Which would help more: a different kind of question, or you telling me in your own words what your job on the airspace desk involves?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: Thank you, that gives me something to work with. Can you give me one recent closure as an example? Tell me what it was, how it came to you, and how you worked out the disruption it caused.

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's fine. Let's skip the specific example. When you enter a closure into the shared picture, what information do you have to put in, step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try something different. What part of the job frustrates you most?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You've said "I don't know" several times now, and I'd rather adjust my approach than keep asking questions that aren't working. Would it help if I asked only yes-or-no questions, or would you rather tell me in your own words about whatever part of your work you think matters most?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Let's try a yes-or-no question. Do you personally enter closures into the shared picture, yes or no?

Interviewee: When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers. The authorities announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once, and these are often amended during the day.

Interviewer: Thanks. Do you check amended closures by hand, yes or no?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Have you ever found an amended closure that was wrong or out of date, yes or no?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What would make you trust a system's record of closures more than you trust your own checks?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: I've now asked several questions in different ways, and most answers have been "I don't know." Would you prefer to stop here, or is there a specific part of your work you'd like to describe?

Interviewee: I don't know.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
